subtopic_detail: immunised school aged child with a third episode of one sided swelling in front of the ear
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old boy whose left cheek has swollen up again in front of and below the ear. His mother says it came up over about a day, is uncomfortable rather than agonising, and that the same thing happened twice in the past eighteen months, each time settling over a week or so. On both previous occasions he was given oral antibiotics.

He is fully immunised on the National Immunisation Program schedule and has had no overseas travel or unwell contacts. He is drinking normally and his mouth is not dry, and his eyes are not gritty. On examination he is afebrile and cheerful. There is a tender 4 cm swelling over the left parotid region that lifts the earlobe outward; the right side is normal. The overlying skin is normal in colour and not warm. Milking the duct opposite the upper second molar produces a small amount of clear saliva. Serum amylase is 186 U/L (30 to 110).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees
data_table.Examination: Tender 4 cm left parotid swelling lifting the earlobe, normal overlying skin colour and temperature, right parotid normal
data_table.Duct: Clear saliva expressed from the left Stensen duct orifice on massage, no pus
data_table.Investigations: Serum amylase 186 U/L (30 to 110), full blood examination and C reactive protein within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send a throat swab for mumps polymerase chain reaction and notify the public health unit
options.rationale: Mumps remains notifiable and would be the default for parotid swelling, but it is characteristically bilateral or sequential, occurs once, and is very unlikely in a child fully covered by the measles mumps and rubella schedule. A third episode on the same side is not mumps. (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia)

options.text: Commence oral di flucloxacillin for ten days and review the swelling again in one week
options.rationale: Antistaphylococcal therapy treats acute suppurative parotitis, which occurs in dehydrated or debilitated children with a hot erythematous gland and frank pus expressible from the duct. Clear saliva in an afebrile well child argues against it, and two previous courses have already failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Request anti Ro and anti La antibodies and refer him to a paediatric rheumatologist
options.rationale: Juvenile Sjogren syndrome is the systemic mimic worth remembering and does cause recurrent parotid swelling, but it is far commoner in adolescent girls and is accompanied by dry eyes and a dry mouth. Normal salivary flow and no ocular symptoms make it improbable as a first line test. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Sjogren syndrome)

options.text: Arrange an ultrasound of both parotid glands and advise massage with sialogogues
options.rationale: Recurrent unilateral parotid swelling in a well immunised child with clear ductal saliva is juvenile recurrent parotitis, and ultrasound showing multiple small hypoechoic sialectatic areas confirms it without radiation. Management is conservative with hydration, gland massage and sialogogues during attacks. (Source: RCH CPG: Parotitis)

options.text: Request serum lipase with an abdominal ultrasound to investigate the raised amylase
options.rationale: The amylase here is salivary in origin, which is the trap: any inflamed salivary gland raises total amylase without pancreatic disease, and this boy has no abdominal pain or vomiting. Lipase would be normal and the imaging would be negative. (Source: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia)
source_refs: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia

explanation.summary: Juvenile recurrent parotitis is the second commonest cause of parotid swelling in children after mumps and presents with repeated episodes of unilateral or alternating parotid inflammation between the ages of three and six. The pathology is non obstructive sialectasis with ductal ectasia, and each attack lasts days to a couple of weeks before settling spontaneously. Three conditions have to be reasoned past: mumps, which is usually bilateral and does not recur in an immunised child; acute suppurative parotitis, which is febrile with purulent ductal discharge; and an autoimmune sialadenitis, which brings sicca symptoms. A raised total amylase is expected and reflects the salivary isoenzyme, so it should not trigger a pancreatic workup. Ultrasound is the imaging of choice and most children outgrow the condition by puberty, with sialendoscopy reserved for frequent disabling attacks.
key_points: Recurrent unilateral parotid swelling in a well immunised child is rarely mumps.
Clear ductal saliva and an afebrile child argue against suppurative parotitis.
Total amylase rises from the salivary isoenzyme and does not indicate pancreatitis.
Ultrasound showing sialectasis confirms the diagnosis without radiation.
Most cases resolve spontaneously around puberty with conservative management.
explanation.pearls: Splitting total amylase into pancreatic and salivary isoenzymes, or simply checking a lipase, resolves the diagnostic confusion in minutes: lipase is normal in salivary disease because the salivary glands do not produce it.

sources.label: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia

subtopic_detail: young woman with bleeding after intercourse and a red ring around the cervical opening on speculum
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 23-year-old woman who has had light bleeding after sex on about six occasions over the past four months. It is bright red, lasts a few hours, and is not associated with pain. She has been taking a combined oral contraceptive pill for two years and has no intermenstrual bleeding otherwise.

She has one regular partner of three years and no history of sexually transmitted infection. Her cervical screening test four months ago was negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus. On speculum examination the vagina is healthy with no discharge, and there is a symmetrical circumferential area of red velvety tissue extending from the external os onto the surrounding cervix, which bleeds lightly when touched with the swab. There is no visible growth or ulceration, the cervix is smooth in outline, and bimanual examination is non tender with no adnexal mass. A self collected vaginal swab for chlamydia and gonorrhoea is negative.

data_table.Examination: Circumferential red velvety area around the external os that bleeds on contact, no growth or ulceration
data_table.Bimanual: Mobile non tender uterus of normal size, no adnexal mass or cervical excitation
data_table.Investigations: Human papillomavirus testing negative four months ago, chlamydia and gonorrhoea nucleic acid testing negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Treat empirically with doxycycline for two weeks and repeat the swabs after completion
options.rationale: Empirical doxycycline covers chlamydial cervicitis, the important infective near pair, which produces a mucopurulent discharge and a friable inflamed cervix rather than a sharply demarcated symmetrical red zone. Her swabs are already negative. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer urgently for colposcopic assessment of the cervix with directed biopsy of the area
options.rationale: Urgent colposcopy is mandatory when the cervix looks suspicious, with an irregular growth, ulceration or a friable mass, because human papillomavirus testing alone never excludes cancer in that setting. A smooth symmetrical ectropion in a woman with recent negative testing is not that cervix. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines)

options.text: Repeat the cervical screening test today as a clinician collected sample and await results
options.rationale: Repeating a negative oncogenic human papillomavirus test four months on adds nothing, since the test interval is five years and the virus does not clear and reappear that quickly. The finding needing explanation is the visible one. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines)

options.text: Arrange cryotherapy or diathermy ablation of the cervix at her next available appointment
options.rationale: Ablation is reserved for an ectropion causing persistent troublesome bleeding or discharge after conservative measures have been tried. Treating at first presentation exposes her to a procedure that many women avoid simply by changing contraceptive method. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

options.text: Explain the finding, offer a change to a non oestrogen method, and review in three months
options.rationale: A symmetrical columnar epithelial area around the os in a young woman on oestrogen containing contraception is a cervical ectropion, a benign physiological finding that bleeds on contact. With infection and oncogenic human papillomavirus excluded, explanation with a contraceptive change is appropriate before any ablative treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

explanation.summary: Cervical ectropion describes columnar endocervical epithelium lying on the ectocervix, where it appears as a red velvety zone around the external os and bleeds easily because the epithelium is a single cell layer thick. It is physiological and is promoted by oestrogen, so it is commonest in adolescence, pregnancy and among users of combined hormonal contraception. The clinical trap is that postcoital bleeding is also the presenting symptom of cervical cancer and of chlamydial cervicitis, so neither can be dismissed on the appearance alone. Australian screening guidance is explicit that a symptomatic woman with a visibly abnormal or suspicious cervix is referred for colposcopy regardless of her human papillomavirus result, because the test screens for risk rather than diagnosing an established lesion. Where the cervix is smooth and symmetrical, infection has been excluded and screening is up to date, explanation with a change of contraception is first line, and ablation is reserved for persistent symptoms.
key_points: Oestrogen exposure promotes ectropion, so combined contraception and pregnancy are common contexts.
Exclude chlamydial cervicitis and confirm screening status before attributing bleeding to it.
A visibly suspicious cervix warrants colposcopy whatever the human papillomavirus result.
First line management is explanation with consideration of a non oestrogen method.
Ablative treatment is reserved for persistent troublesome symptoms.
explanation.pearls: The rule that catches people out is that a negative oncogenic human papillomavirus test does not exclude cervical cancer in a woman with abnormal bleeding, because around five per cent of cervical cancers, particularly adenocarcinomas, are not detected by screening; the appearance of the cervix decides the referral.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

subtopic_detail: frothy yellow green vaginal discharge with motile organisms reported on a self collected swab
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29-year-old woman with three weeks of an offensive yellow green vaginal discharge and soreness on passing urine. She describes the discharge as frothy and says it has an unpleasant smell that has not responded to an over the counter antifungal pessary.

She has a new male partner of two months and uses condoms inconsistently. Her last cervical screening test was negative eighteen months ago and she is not pregnant, confirmed by a urinary test today. On speculum examination there is an adherent frothy discharge coating the vaginal walls and the vaginal pH measured with indicator paper is 5.5. The cervix appears inflamed with scattered punctate haemorrhages. Bimanual examination reveals no cervical excitation, no adnexal tenderness and a normal sized mobile uterus. A self collected vaginal swab reports Trichomonas vaginalis detected by nucleic acid amplification, with chlamydia and gonorrhoea not detected.

data_table.Examination: Adherent frothy yellow green discharge, vaginal pH 5.5, cervix with punctate haemorrhages
data_table.Bimanual: No cervical excitation, no adnexal tenderness, mobile normal sized uterus
data_table.Investigations: Trichomonas vaginalis detected on nucleic acid amplification, chlamydia and gonorrhoea not detected, urinary pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a single dose of oral fluconazole and review her symptoms again in two weeks
options.rationale: Single dose fluconazole has no activity against protozoa and simply repeats the failed self treatment in a different formulation. It also delays partner notification by a fortnight. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Prescribe intravaginal clotrimazole for six nights and advise avoidance of soaps and bubble baths
options.rationale: Topical azole therapy treats vulvovaginal candidiasis, which gives a thick white non offensive discharge with a normal vaginal pH below 4.5 and intense itch. The raised pH and frothy offensive discharge point away from yeast, and she has already failed an antifungal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Prescribe oral metronidazole for her and arrange treatment of her current sexual partner
options.rationale: Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted protozoal infection, so oral nitroimidazole therapy for the patient plus partner treatment is required to prevent immediate reinfection. Treating the index case alone is the commonest reason for apparent treatment failure. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

options.text: Prescribe intramuscular ceftriaxone with oral azithromycin and repeat testing in three months
options.rationale: This is the regimen for gonococcal infection, which has already been excluded by nucleic acid testing, and neither agent has useful antiprotozoal activity. Empirical dual therapy here treats an organism that is not present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Prescribe intravaginal metronidazole gel nightly for five nights without partner treatment
options.rationale: Intravaginal metronidazole reaches useful concentrations in the vagina but not in the urethra and periurethral glands where the organism also lives, so cure rates are substantially lower than with oral therapy. It is the near pair that fails through inadequate site coverage. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Trichomonas vaginalis is a flagellated protozoan transmitted sexually and is the only one of the three common causes of vaginal discharge that requires partner treatment. The classic picture is a frothy offensive yellow green discharge with a vaginal pH above 4.5 and a cervix showing punctate haemorrhages, although a substantial proportion of infections are asymptomatic in both sexes. Nucleic acid amplification has largely replaced wet mount microscopy because sensitivity is far higher, particularly on self collected vaginal swabs. Oral nitroimidazole therapy is required rather than intravaginal treatment because the organism colonises the urethra and periurethral glands, which topical preparations do not reach. In Australia trichomoniasis is substantially more prevalent in remote communities than in urban settings, which matters for both testing thresholds and for follow up.
key_points: Vaginal pH above 4.5 separates trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis from candidiasis.
Nucleic acid amplification on a vaginal swab is far more sensitive than wet mount microscopy.
Oral therapy is required because topical treatment misses the urethral reservoir.
Partner treatment is mandatory to prevent prompt reinfection.
Screen for other sexually transmitted infections including syphilis and blood borne viruses.
explanation.pearls: Trichomoniasis in pregnancy is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight, and metronidazole is not contraindicated at any gestation, so a positive result in a pregnant woman is treated rather than deferred to the postnatal period.

subtopic_detail: smooth red finger of tissue protruding through the cervical opening found at a routine screening visit
stem:
You are the general practitioner performing a routine cervical screening test on a 47-year-old woman. She mentions that she has noticed some spotting between periods over the last six months, which she had put down to approaching menopause, and occasional light bleeding after sex.

Her periods remain regular at 28 days and are not heavy. She has two children, takes no hormonal treatment, and her previous screening tests have all been negative. On speculum examination there is a smooth red finger of tissue about 15 mm long protruding through the external os on a narrow stalk. It bleeds lightly when the swab brushes it. The remainder of the cervix looks normal with no ulceration or irregularity, and the vaginal walls are healthy. Bimanual examination reveals a mobile anteverted uterus of normal size with no adnexal masses, and the human papillomavirus result returns negative for oncogenic types.

data_table.Examination: Smooth pedunculated 15 mm red lesion protruding through the external os, bleeding on contact
data_table.Bimanual: Mobile anteverted uterus of normal size, no adnexal mass, no cervical excitation
data_table.Investigations: Human papillomavirus testing negative for oncogenic types

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Avulse the lesion in the treatment room today and discard it after the bleeding settles
options.rationale: Simple avulsion in the consulting room is a reasonable technique for a small polyp on a thin stalk, but discarding the specimen forfeits the histology that is the whole point of removing it. Any tissue removed must go to pathology. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

options.text: Refer urgently under the suspected cancer pathway for examination under anaesthesia and staging
options.rationale: Urgent cancer referral is the response to a hard irregular friable growth or a barrel shaped cervix, the near pair that cannot be distinguished at the bedside from a benign polyp only by guesswork. A smooth pedunculated lesion on a narrow stalk with an otherwise normal cervix does not meet that threshold. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Cervical cancer)

options.text: Reassure her that these are benign findings and repeat her screening test in five years
options.rationale: Most cervical polyps are benign, but reassurance alone leaves a symptomatic lesion in place without tissue diagnosis and ignores six months of abnormal bleeding in a woman approaching menopause. The negative screening result speaks to human papillomavirus risk rather than to this lesion. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines)

options.text: Commence a combined oral contraceptive pill to regulate the bleeding and review in six months
options.rationale: Hormonal suppression addresses dysfunctional bleeding once structural causes have been excluded, and a visible bleeding lesion is a structural cause. Masking her symptom for six months delays the diagnosis. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

options.text: Refer for removal of the lesion with histopathology and assessment of the endometrial cavity
options.rationale: A pedunculated cervical polyp explains intermenstrual and postcoital bleeding and should be removed and sent for histology, since a small proportion harbour malignancy. Endometrial assessment is added because cervical polyps often coexist with endometrial polyps and her bleeding pattern needs the cavity evaluated. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

explanation.summary: Cervical polyps are benign overgrowths of endocervical tissue found in around four per cent of women, most often between the ages of forty and sixty. They present with intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, or are found incidentally at speculum examination, and their fragile surface epithelium accounts for the contact bleeding. Malignancy is rare, of the order of one in a thousand, but it is not predictable from appearance, so every removed polyp goes to histopathology. Because cervical and endometrial polyps frequently coexist and abnormal uterine bleeding in a woman in her forties requires the cavity to be assessed, removal is usually combined with hysteroscopy or transvaginal ultrasound rather than done in isolation. A cervix that looks irregular, ulcerated or friable is a different problem and requires colposcopy or urgent gynaecological oncology referral regardless of screening results.
key_points: Cervical polyps cause intermenstrual and postcoital bleeding through contact bleeding.
Malignancy is rare but unpredictable, so all removed tissue goes to histopathology.
Cervical and endometrial polyps often coexist, so assess the cavity as well.
A negative screening test does not explain or exclude a visible cervical lesion.
An irregular ulcerated friable cervix requires colposcopy or urgent referral instead.
explanation.pearls: Abnormal uterine bleeding is classified by the FIGO PALM COEIN system, in which polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma and malignancy are the structural causes visible on imaging or histology, and remembering that a visible polyp is the P of PALM is what stops it being managed as dysfunctional bleeding.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

subtopic_detail: adolescent with monthly lower abdominal pain who has never had a period and a bulging bluish membrane
stem:
You are the registrar in a paediatric emergency department seeing a 14-year-old girl brought in by her mother with lower abdominal pain. The pain has come in episodes lasting three or four days roughly every month for the past six months and is worsening; this time she has also found it difficult to pass urine and has not opened her bowels for two days.

She has never had a period. Her mother reports that she developed breasts around the age of eleven and that her growth spurt is finished. On examination she is afebrile and comfortable at rest. Breast development and pubic hair are both Tanner stage 5. There is a smooth, non tender midline suprapubic mass that reaches halfway to the umbilicus. Inspection of the vulva shows normal external genitalia with a tense bluish membrane bulging at the introitus, which becomes more prominent when she coughs. A bladder scan shows a residual volume of 480 mL.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 5 breast and pubic hair development, smooth non tender midline suprapubic mass
data_table.Vulval inspection: Normal external genitalia with a tense bluish membrane bulging at the introitus, more prominent on coughing
data_table.Investigations: Post void bladder residual volume 480 mL on bedside scan, urinary pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence a continuous combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress her cyclical symptoms
options.rationale: Menstrual suppression is a legitimate temporising measure when definitive surgery must be delayed, which is why it is tempting here. It does nothing for an existing collection or for the retention it is causing, so it cannot be the primary step. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Request a karyotype with serum testosterone and refer to the adolescent gynaecology clinic
options.rationale: Karyotype and androgen testing investigate complete androgen insensitivity, the near pair that also presents with primary amenorrhoea and normal breast development. That condition gives absent or sparse pubic hair and a blind ending vagina without an obstructed distended collection. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea)

options.text: Aspirate the collection through the membrane in the department with a wide bore needle
options.rationale: Needle aspiration decompresses the collection briefly but leaves the obstruction intact, so it refills, and puncturing a closed space risks converting sterile old blood into a pyocolpos. Formal incision with drainage is the standard. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Imperforate hymen)

options.text: Insert a urinary catheter and refer for surgical incision of the obstructing membrane
options.rationale: Primary amenorrhoea with normal secondary sexual characteristics, cyclical pain and a bulging bluish membrane is an imperforate hymen with haematocolpos, and urinary retention makes it urgent. Catheterisation relieves the retention while definitive surgical hymenotomy under anaesthesia drains the obstruction. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea)

options.text: Arrange an outpatient pelvic ultrasound and gynaecology clinic review within four weeks
options.rationale: Outpatient imaging would be sensible for cyclical pain without retention, and ultrasound does confirm the diagnosis. Waiting a month with a bladder residual of 480 mL risks upper tract dilatation and continued retrograde menstruation. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea)

explanation.summary: Imperforate hymen is the commonest obstructive anomaly of the female genital tract and results from failure of the hymenal membrane to canalise at the junction of the sinovaginal bulb and urogenital sinus. Because ovarian function and the endometrium are normal, girls develop normally through puberty and present only when menstrual blood accumulates, typically at thirteen to fifteen years with cyclical pain and primary amenorrhoea. Accumulated blood distends the vagina and later the uterus, producing a palpable pelvic mass that can compress the bladder neck and cause acute urinary retention, or the rectum and cause constipation. The examination that makes the diagnosis is simple inspection of the vulva, which is why the condition is often missed for months when the abdomen alone is examined. Definitive treatment is surgical hymenotomy under general anaesthesia, and outcomes including future fertility are excellent once the obstruction is relieved.
key_points: Normal secondary sexual characteristics with cyclical pain and no menses is the classic triad.
Vulval inspection shows a tense bulging bluish membrane and makes the diagnosis.
Urinary retention or constipation reflects mass effect from the distended vagina.
Androgen insensitivity is the near pair but gives absent pubic hair and no collection.
Definitive management is surgical hymenotomy, not aspiration.
explanation.pearls: Any adolescent presenting with acute urinary retention and no neurological cause should have the vulva inspected before imaging is ordered, because haematocolpos from an imperforate hymen is the diagnosis that a two minute examination makes and an abdominal examination alone will miss.
